opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's the one we think about more than any other. I don't see task-specific training and generalization as opposites. I see the specific tasks as the path to the general model.

Think about how language models came about. Nobody sat down and wrote a general theory of language. You trained on an enormous, diverse body of text, and the generalization emerged from the breadth. The problem in robotics is that there's no internet of robot data. There's no giant corpus of physical interaction just sitting there to scrape. So you have to generate it, and the most practical way to generate high-quality physical data is to put robots to work on real tasks that people actually care about and will pay for.

When a robot picks items in a warehouse, folds laundry, or loads a dishwasher, each of those looks narrow on its own. But underneath, they share a lot of structure. Grasping deformable versus rigid objects, handling occlusion, recovering when something slips, reasoning about where things are in 3D space, understanding cause and effect when you push or pull. Every task exercises some subset of those primitive skills. If you train one model across many tasks, rather than a separate model per task, it starts learning those shared primitives instead of memorizing a single workflow.

What we've seen, and what a lot of the field is starting to see, is positive transfer. You add a new task, and the model picks it up faster because it already learned something relevant elsewhere. Eventually you hit a point where you can show it a handful of demonstrations, or even just describe the task in language, and it gets most of the way there. That's when it starts to feel like a foundation model rather than a collection of skills.

The other piece is deployment as a data flywheel. Robots out in the real world hit edge cases you'd never script in a lab: weird lighting, a cup someone left in the wrong place, a box that's slightly crushed. Those failures are incredibly valuable. You capture them, sometimes with a human stepping in remotely to correct, and that feeds back into training. The more robots you have doing useful work, the more diverse your data, and the more general the model becomes.

So my short answer is that generality is earned through specificity at scale. You don't skip the specific tasks. You do many of them with one shared model, you deploy it where it creates real value so the data keeps coming, and over time the narrow skills compound into something much broader. I don't think anyone has fully cracked it yet, but I think that's the most credible path there.

r001.rationale: The response says robots should generate physical data by performing useful real tasks, then train one model across many tasks so shared skills support broader generalization.

r002.rationale: It compares robot training to language-model training, but does not mention Tesla or data collected during human driving.

r003.rationale: It explains that real-world deployments encounter varied conditions—such as unusual lighting, misplaced objects, and damaged boxes—and that these edge cases add diverse training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's the question everyone in the field is wrestling with right now. The way I think about it is that specific tasks are the data engine, not the end goal.

So when we train a robot to do something narrow, say picking parts out of a bin or folding a towel, what we're really doing is collecting a very rich stream of data about how perception connects to action in the physical world. Every one of those demonstrations teaches the model something about contact, about friction, about what happens when you grasp an object slightly off-center. Those lessons aren't really about towels. They're about physics and manipulation in general.

And the thing we've seen, which mirrors what happened in language, is that once you aggregate enough of those narrow tasks across enough embodiments and environments, the model starts to pick up shared structure. It learns a kind of common grammar of manipulation. So a robot that's been trained on a few hundred tasks will often handle a new object or a new scene with surprisingly little additional data, because it's not starting from zero anymore. It's recognizing that this new thing looks a lot like problems it has already solved.

Now, I want to be honest about where the analogy to language models breaks down. With text, the internet gave us a free, enormous dataset. Robotics doesn't have that. Every real-world trajectory costs time, hardware, and often a human teleoperator. So the specific tasks matter twice over. They're commercially valuable on their own, which pays for the data collection, and they feed the foundation model that makes the next task cheaper to learn. That flywheel is really the whole business case.

The other piece I'd emphasize is diversity over volume. A million repetitions of the same task in the same lab doesn't get you much generalization. A thousand tasks across messy, real customer sites, with different lighting, different fixtures, different failure modes, gets you a lot further. So when we choose which tasks to go after, we're thinking about what new slice of the physical world each one exposes the model to.

Where I think this lands over the next few years is a model that you don't retrain for each deployment so much as you prompt or lightly fine-tune. You show it a handful of examples of the new job and it fills in the rest from everything it's seen before. We're not fully there yet, but the trajectory from narrow task to general capability is looking a lot more like a continuum than a leap.

r001.rationale: It describes narrow-task demonstrations as rich data linking perception to action and says the aggregated data supports a foundation model that generalizes to new tasks.

r002.rationale: It compares the approach to language-model training, but does not mention Tesla or data gathered during human driving for autonomous driving.

r003.rationale: It explains that tasks across real customer sites expose the model to differing lighting, fixtures, and failure modes, producing diverse data.

astra-6.text:
I think you get there by starting with specific tasks and getting robots to do them reliably in the real world. Even something that sounds simple, like picking up an object, involves perception, movement, grasping, and understanding whether you actually succeeded.

As you train across more tasks, you want the model to reuse those capabilities. Picking up a cup and picking up a tool are different jobs, but there’s a lot of shared understanding underneath them. The question is whether each new task requires you to start over, or whether the robot can build on what it already knows.

That’s the path toward generalization: a shared model that learns from a broad range of real interactions and needs progressively less training for something new. It’s not automatic just because you’ve collected a lot of task data. You have to test it in unfamiliar situations and see whether that knowledge actually transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says to train robots across tasks and learn from real interactions, but does not clearly identify data collected by robots performing specific tasks as the basis for training.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy to Tesla or to data collected during human driving.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that similar tasks produce varied data because real-world execution conditions differ.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you get there by training on specific tasks, but making sure the robot is learning something it can reuse. Picking up a cup and picking up a tool are different tasks, but they share a lot: understanding where an object is, how to grasp it, how much force to apply, and whether the action worked.

As you build up those experiences across different objects and environments, the question becomes: can the model take what it learned in one situation and apply it to another? Can it handle a cup it hasn’t seen before, or a workspace where things have moved?

That’s why deployment matters. A task that looks simple in a demonstration gets much more complicated when you have to do it reliably every day. Those variations and failures give you the training signal to improve the model. So specific tasks are the starting point. Generalization comes from learning the shared capabilities underneath them, and then testing whether those capabilities transfer.

r001.rationale: It describes training on specific tasks and accumulating experiences, but does not identify data collected by robots performing those tasks as the training basis.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to Tesla or to human-driving data used for autonomous-driving training.

r003.rationale: It says deployment brings variations and failures that can improve the model, but does not clearly state that deploying robots on similar tasks produces varied data because real-world execution conditions differ.
